decisoes_da_sala_aplicadas: O vazio: 'fewer than 1,500' sempre com 'the census district' (gancho S3 e a última frase do vídeo); o distrito demarcado no mapa a cada vez que um número dele é dito; o p1 inteiro é a régua (dois terços da costa, o sul noutro distrito); 70 milhas só no p1, longe de qualquer 1.500; nunca 'the town of Big Sur', 'zero people', 'nobody lives here'.
O Wyoming: 'as empty as Wyoming' (gancho) e 'about six people per square mile' (p1), 2020 com 2020 ('The count itself is from 2020, the most recent census').
As metrópoles: 'Los Angeles and San Francisco', pelo nome, e 'Their metro areas hold more than 17 million people'; nunca 'largest' nem 'biggest'.

Os anos 1880: 'nearly a thousand', atribuído ao plano de 1986 e dito da costa ('The same plan says nearly a thousand people lived along this coast by the 1880s'; p4: 'That count is for the whole coast in the plan, not just the census district'); nunca comparado com hoje por palavra.

A estrada: 1919 com a FHWA, 'nearly two decades', 1937 por cerca de US$ 8 milhões (o plano), presos de três acampamentos de San Quentin a 35 centavos por dia e com a pena reduzida (FHWA): 'Part of the labor came from prisoners'.

A regra de 1986: sempre no passado ('made it policy', 'had to be moved', 'remained possible'); o 'critical viewshed' definido; os 15 % parafraseados; 'about half ... public land' (o 60 % fora); nada de 'still', 'today' ou 'since 1986' sobre ela.

O hoje: Paul's Slide (janeiro de 2023), Regent's Slide (fevereiro de 2024, seis milhas ao norte), 'For almost three years', a reabertura em 14/01/2026; o Timber Fire em palavras e com dono (CAL FIRE e Caltrans), 'hundreds of homes, businesses and other buildings' ameaçados, trechos fechados 'inside the census district' 'for weeks', o Plaskett só pelo nome; a estrada aberta em novembro de 2026 com mão única em obras. Nunca 'destroyed', 'third-largest' nem 'the road is closed' no presente.

As casas: duas réguas, cada uma com o dono (o dia do censo de 2020, 'almost four in ten'; a pesquisa de 5 anos do Census Bureau, 2020–2024, 'nearly all ... seasonal, recreational or occasional use'); nenhum número com margem na voz; a Califórnia, 'about a third'.
Os visitantes: 2,9 milhões com 1986; em 2026, 'Caltrans reported that the visitors came back'; nenhum número de visitantes de hoje; o 900 % fica fora.

Fora: o preço das casas, as mansões, os bilionários, os Esselen, a falha, o terremoto, a neblina, 'the strictest plan', 'California's emptiest coast', 'the only road' (o p2 diz o contrário: 'just one other road from inland').

Do vídeo 5 em diante: frases curtas (média 12,2 no esqueleto; a maior, 23), um número por frase, o vídeo de ~2.330 palavras (12,7 min a 184; 15,5 min a 150), nenhum título de capítulo na tela, mais mapa e mais animação sobre o mapa.
pergunta: Why is the census district around Big Sur, on the coast between Los Angeles and San Francisco, as empty as Wyoming, when nearly a thousand people already lived on this coast in the 1880s?
pergunta_no_gancho: Duas, curtas: 'Why?' (S4, palavra 36 da cópia para a voz com 'fifteen hundred', 14,4 s a 150 palavras/min) e 'So why didn't more follow?' (S9, a segunda virada, palavra ~78 da voz, ~31 s a 150). A segunda é a pergunta do gancho para o portão (a última frase com '?' antes da assinatura); nenhuma sequência de 5 palavras dela volta no fecho.

tese.frase: O distrito do censo de Big Sur tem a densidade do Wyoming não pelo clima nem por falta de quem viesse, mas porque três camadas se somam, cada uma medida pelo seu dono: a terra deixa pouco lugar para morar (a serra que cai no mar, o solo que desliza, a água pouca e sazonal, e metade da área do plano em floresta nacional e área selvagem); a história fez da costa um lugar de passagem (quase mil pessoas viviam do que mandavam por mar nos anos 1880; a estrada só ficou pronta em 1937, depois de quase duas décadas, e trouxe visitantes; o plano do condado de 1986 proibiu o novo que se vê da Highway 1 e guardou a maior parte da estrada para a recreação); e o hoje mantém o padrão (a estrada fechada por quase três anos e de novo no fogo de 2026, casas que existem e ficam vazias, quase todas de uso ocasional, e visitantes que voltam e seguem viagem). O vazio é um vazio de moradores: contado por casas ou por carros, esta costa não é vazia.
o_que_nao_diz: que a regra de 1986 criou o vazio: a costa já era pouco povoada antes (o p6 diz 'The rule didn't empty this coast');
que a população não cresceu desde os anos 1880, que é 'a mesma' ou que é menor: os quase mil são da costa do plano, e o 1.474 é de parte dela;
que construir é proibido: só o novo que se vê da estrada e dos mirantes; o resto, com condições;
que a regra vale igual hoje (não confirmado, pauta §11, item 2);
que ninguém mora lá, ou que é 'a cidade de Big Sur';
que o fogo destruiu casas, ou qualquer número do fogo na voz;
que as casas vazias são de ricos, mansões ou casas de bilionários; o preço das casas;
que é a costa mais vazia da Califórnia, ou o plano mais rígido do país;
que a Highway 1 é a única estrada;

promessa: Explicar por que um pedaço da costa da Califórnia, entre as regiões metropolitanas de Los Angeles e de San Francisco (mais de 17 milhões), tem um distrito do censo com menos de 1.500 pessoas, tão vazio quanto o Wyoming, se não é o clima e se já havia quase mil pessoas nesta costa nos anos 1880; e mostrar o que esse 'vazio' mede.

payoff.resposta: A terra: a serra que cai no mar, sem chão para cidade nem porto, a terra que desliza, a água pouca e sazonal, e metade da área do plano em floresta nacional e área selvagem (p2–p3). A história: a gente dos anos 1880 vivia pelo mar; a estrada chegou tarde (1919–1937, com presos), acabou com um modo de vida e trouxe gente de passagem; o plano de 1986 proibiu o novo que se vê da estrada e guardou a estrada para os visitantes (p4–p6). O hoje: a estrada que fecha (2023–2026; o fogo de 2026), as casas que existem e ficam vazias, quase todas de uso ocasional, e os visitantes que voltam e seguem (p7–p8). A virada da régua: contado por moradores, é o Wyoming; por casas, cabe mais gente; por carros, o condado já racionava a estrada em 1986 (p8). O fecho volta à ponte, entre as duas metrópoles, com os nomes dos colonos no mapa (p9).
payoff.onde: p2 (o clima não é o problema: o chão e o acesso), p3 (metade pública; Mud Creek), p4 (quase mil, pelo mar), p5 (a estrada e o fim de um modo de vida), p6 (a regra do que se vê; a estrada para os visitantes), p7 (quase três anos; o fogo), p8 (as casas de uso ocasional; os visitantes; o que se conta), p9 (o fecho).

gancho.texto:
This is Big Sur, between Los Angeles and San Francisco. Their metro areas hold more than 17 million people. But the census district around this bridge counted fewer than 1,500, as empty as Wyoming. Why?

It isn't the weather. Monterey County's 1986 plan for this coast calls the climate mild. And it isn't that nobody came. The same plan says nearly a thousand people lived along this coast by the 1880s. So why didn't more follow? The mountains are only part of it. The rest is a road that has closed again and again, and a rule about what can be built in sight of it. And then there are the homes that often sit empty. You're at Alpha Point, and this is where the story of the coast that never filled up begins.

Com 'one thousand five hundred' (a forma do vídeo 4 em roteiros/atlantico-fundo/voz/trocas.md), cai na 38 (15,2 s a 150): por isso a recomendação de 'fifteen hundred' na cópia para a voz deste vídeo. Até o 'Why?' não cabe palavra nova.
contagem.segunda_pergunta: 'So why didn't more follow?' fecha na palavra ~78 da voz (~31 s a 150; ~25 s a 184).
contagem.segundos: o gancho tem 134 palavras no texto (~139 na voz): ~44 s a 184 e ~56 s a 150, mais a vinheta. É 14 palavras maior que o gancho A (120): as 10 de 'And then there are the homes that often sit empty.' são o primeiro corte se o gancho precisar encolher (ver 'riscos').

partes.ponte_entrada: Start with what the census actually measured.
beats: O que é o distrito: 'In the United States, every county is divided into smaller census districts. One of them, in Monterey County, is named Big Sur.' (L1, C3: 'Big Sur CCD'; não existe lugar recenseado 'Big Sur')

O contorno: 'It begins a few miles south of Carmel and follows the shore past this bridge, far down the coast. Behind the shore, it climbs into the mountains.' (L1: de ~36,48 N a ~35,99 N, e a serra atrás)

Dois terços e o sul fora: 'Altogether, the district takes in roughly two-thirds of the Big Sur coast. The southern end belongs to a different district, one that reaches over the mountains to a valley inland.' (L1; pauta, 'Três coisas', item 1: o distrito de San Ardo)

A régua dita: 'Every number we give for the census district is about the outline on this map, and nothing wider. The count itself is from 2020, the most recent census.' (o aviso dos leitores 1; 2020 com 2020)
A densidade: 'The Big Sur district has about 250 square miles of land. Spread its people across all of it. You get about six people per square mile.' (C3, L1: 251,4 mi²; conta: 5,86/mi²)

O Wyoming e a Califórnia: 'Wyoming has about the same. No state in the US outside Alaska has fewer people for its size. California, the most populous state in the country, is more than 40 times as crowded.' (C1, C2: 5,94/mi², o menos denso dos 48 contíguos; C3: 253,7/mi², 43×, conta)

A segunda régua: 'The county's plan uses a longer ruler. It covers the whole coast, more than 70 miles, from Carmel down to the next county. Keep both outlines in mind, because they don't describe the same ground.' (P: 'over seventy miles in length', 'from the Carmel area on the north, south to the San Luis Obispo County line'; nenhum 1.500 no p1)
partes.o_que_o_espectador_entende: Que o número é real e tem contorno: um distrito do censo que cobre uns dois terços da costa (ao norte, mais a serra), com uns 250 mi² e umas seis pessoas por milha quadrada, como o Wyoming, num estado mais de 40 vezes mais cheio; e que o plano de 1986, que o vídeo vai citar, fala de uma costa maior. Ainda não sabe por quê.

partes.voz_do_esqueleto:
Start with what the census actually measured. In the United States, every county is divided into smaller census districts. One of them, in Monterey County, is named Big Sur. It begins a few miles south of Carmel and follows the shore past this bridge, far down the coast. Behind the shore, it climbs into the mountains.

Altogether, the district takes in roughly two-thirds of the Big Sur coast. The southern end belongs to a different district, one that reaches over the mountains to a valley inland. Every number we give for the census district is about the outline on this map, and nothing wider. The count itself is from 2020, the most recent census.

The Big Sur district has about 250 square miles of land. Spread its people across all of it. You get about six people per square mile. Wyoming has about the same. No state in the US outside Alaska has fewer people for its size. California, the most populous state in the country, is more than 40 times as crowded.

The county's plan uses a longer ruler. It covers the whole coast, more than 70 miles, from Carmel down to the next county. Keep both outlines in mind, because they don't describe the same ground. To see why the census number is so low, start with the ground itself.

partes.titulo: Mountains that drop into the sea
partes.funcao: demonstrar o primeiro mecanismo (ato 1, a física): a serra que cai no mar, a lista dos limites do plano (a água, o acesso, o solo instável, o fogo e a enchente), o acesso por uma estrada e meia, e a água pouca; paga o 'It isn't the weather' do gancho e planta o fogo para o p7.
partes.ponte_entrada: So what makes this ground so hard to live on?
beats: A pergunta do ato 1 e a serra: 'Behind the coast rise the Santa Lucia Mountains. At Cone Peak, near the southern end of the coast, they reach 5,200 feet. The county's plan says their western slopes drop precipitously to the sea.' (P [53]; o Cone Peak fica no distrito de San Ardo: 'near the southern end of the coast', nunca 'in the district')
O chão: 'That leaves little flat ground for a town, or for a port.' (a leitura da pauta §7 do 'drop precipitously')
A frase-mãe do ato: 'The plan lists what holds building back: water, difficult access, unstable soils on steep slopes, and the dangers of fire and flood.' (P [71]; o fogo plantado para o p7)

O acesso: 'Highway 1, the plan says, is the basic route in and out. In 1986, it counted just one other road from inland. That one is a lightly used county road that climbs over the mountains and crosses a military reservation.' (P [1291]–[1293]: a Nacimiento–Fergusson; é o contrário de 'the only road')

A água: 'Nearly fifty separate streams run down these mountains, according to the plan. Yet it calls the water resources small and seasonal. That same water has to support the animals, the plants and the people.' (P; P [188])

O clima volta: 'The weather, remember, is mild. The trouble is finding ground where a house can stand, and a way to reach it. That's one reason the census district holds so few people per square mile.' ('one reason', nunca 'the reason')
partes.o_que_o_espectador_entende: Que a serra cai direto no mar e não sobra chão plano; que o próprio plano do condado lista os limites (água, acesso, solo, fogo e enchente); que só há a Highway 1 e uma estrada de serra para chegar; que há riacho mas pouca água o ano todo; e que o clima ameno não é o problema. É uma razão, não a única.

Os riachos acesos e apagados no beat da água. O distrito acende inteiro no 'census district' do fim.

partes.voz_do_esqueleto:
So what makes this ground so hard to live on? Behind the coast rise the Santa Lucia Mountains. At Cone Peak, near the southern end of the coast, they reach 5,200 feet. The county's plan says their western slopes drop precipitously to the sea. That leaves little flat ground for a town, or for a port.

The plan lists what holds building back: water, difficult access, unstable soils on steep slopes, and the dangers of fire and flood.

Take access. Highway 1, the plan says, is the basic route in and out. In 1986, it counted just one other road from inland. That one is a lightly used county road that climbs over the mountains and crosses a military reservation.

Then there's water, which sounds like the odd one out. Nearly fifty separate streams run down these mountains, according to the plan. Yet it calls the water resources small and seasonal. That same water has to support the animals, the plants and the people. There's plenty of it running in the wet months, and much less to count on in the dry ones.

The weather, remember, is mild. The trouble is finding ground where a house can stand, and a way to reach it. That's one reason the census district holds so few people per square mile. The other reasons have more to do with who owns the land, and what happened on it.

Metade pública: 'By 1986, about half of the coastal zone was public land, according to the plan.' (L3, P [1514]; o 60 % fica fora)

O tempo sem a estrada e o conserto: 'For almost three years, you couldn't drive this coast from end to end. Crews drilled thousands of steel bars into the slope at Regent's Slide to hold it in place. Caltrans reopened the road there at noon on January 14, 2026. The repair was long and expensive, and it finished months ahead of its target date.' (L5; leituras da Sala §3: as 4.600 barras e os US$ 82,6 milhões só na tela)
Sem alarme: 'Even then, Caltrans warned drivers to expect occasional full closures while crews cleared debris.' (L5; nunca 'it will close again')

partes.voz_do_esqueleto:
So what happens to a coast like this when its road breaks? In January 2023, Paul's Slide closed Highway 1. In February 2024, Regent's Slide gave way, six miles to the north. Paul's Slide reopened that summer, but Regent's kept the road cut.

For almost three years, you couldn't drive this coast from end to end. Crews drilled thousands of steel bars into the slope at Regent's Slide to hold it in place. Caltrans reopened the road there at noon on January 14, 2026. The repair was long and expensive, and it finished months ahead of its target date. Even then, Caltrans warned drivers to expect occasional full closures while crews cleared debris.

Fire was on the county's list of dangers, too. In August 2026, a wildfire started in the national forest above the coast. It became known as the Timber Fire, and it spread through these mountains. Air tankers from across California flew missions over the ridges. The state fire agency listed hundreds of homes, businesses and other buildings as threatened. Firefighters were hurt fighting it. By mid-October, it was almost fully contained.

For weeks, Caltrans kept parts of Highway 1 inside the census district closed. Farther south, a second fire, the Plaskett Fire, closed another stretch. By November 2026, the road was open from end to end again, with one-way traffic at a few work zones. Through all of it, there were homes on this coast. The question is who was living in them.

In 2020, the census district had a little under 900 homes. They're scattered along the ridges, the canyons and the river valley. On census day, almost four in ten of them stood empty.

Empty, on census day, doesn't have to mean abandoned. The Census Bureau also runs a longer survey. Its results for 2020 to 2024 put nearly all of the district's empty homes in one category: seasonal, recreational or occasional use. In other words, they're homes people keep, but don't live in. Across California, homes like that make up about a third of the empty ones. In the census district, an empty home usually means a part-time one.

It isn't a new pattern. In 1976, the plan says, about one home in six on this coast stood empty because it was a second home. Housing was scarce for the people who worked there, too. The 1986 plan noted that some had camped out, lived in cars, or moved in with friends.

The visitors are the other side of the count. After the road reopened in 2026, Caltrans reported that the visitors came back. They come for the view the 1986 plan set out to protect. Then they drive on. The census doesn't count them, because this isn't where they live.

So how empty this coast is depends on what you count. Count the people who live in the census district, and it's as empty as Wyoming. Count the homes, and there's room for more people than live there. Count the cars on Highway 1, and you find a road the county was already rationing in 1986.

presenca.regra: Presença humana é a pessoa ou o grupo que o dossiê documenta, num lugar e num tempo, com o que a fonte diz e nada mais; nunca inventada nem composta.
presenca.a_principal: Os colonos que deram nome ao mapa, num laço entre o p4 e o fecho: Charlie Bixby (o riacho e a ponte do gancho), os Pfeiffer (os parques; John Pfeiffer, que em 1934 vendeu terra ao estado para o núcleo do Pfeiffer Big Sur State Park, o começo da proteção segundo o plano), Jim Anderson e Bill Post (o rancho onde ficaram o primeiro correio e a segunda escola de Big Sur). Fonte: o plano de 1986 (L3, P [1203], [1218]–[1221], [1235]).
as_outras: Godfrey Notley e o povoado de Notley's Landing, no tempo dos desembarcadouros (P [1206]–[1207]); Manchester, a cidade do ouro de Alder Creek nos anos 1880, que começou a minguar em 1895 (P [1213]–[1216], opcional).
Os moradores que, por volta de 1900, guiavam caçadores e pescadores das cidades, e os primeiros visitantes que chegavam de diligência de Monterey (P [1485]–[1487]).
Dr. John Roberts, fundador de Seaside, de quem veio a ideia da estrada aberta o ano todo (P [1227]–[1228]).

Os presos dos três acampamentos de San Quentin (Little Sur River, Kirk Creek e, depois, Anderson Creek), a 35 centavos por dia e com a pena reduzida (FHWA, L4). Sem nomes e sem o ano de chegada (a confirmar).
Os colonos furiosos com as explosões nas encostas (P [1229]–[1231]).
Quem trabalhava na costa em 1986 e às vezes acampava, dormia no carro ou ia morar com amigos, por falta de casa (P [1548]).
Shawn Harrison, pesquisador do USGS, que filmou Mud Creek com drone em 19/07/2017 (L6).

As equipes da Caltrans em Regent's Slide (as barras de aço) e, em 2026, os bombeiros e os aviões-tanque do Timber Fire (DS2: 3 bombeiros feridos; aviões de todo o estado), com as centenas de casas e prédios ameaçados.

esqueleto_medido.texto:
This is Big Sur, between Los Angeles and San Francisco. Their metro areas hold more than 17 million people. But the census district around this bridge counted fewer than 1,500, as empty as Wyoming. Why?

It isn't the weather. Monterey County's 1986 plan for this coast calls the climate mild. And it isn't that nobody came. The same plan says nearly a thousand people lived along this coast by the 1880s. So why didn't more follow? The mountains are only part of it. The rest is a road that has closed again and again, and a rule about what can be built in sight of it. And then there are the homes that often sit empty. You're at Alpha Point, and this is where the story of the coast that never filled up begins.

Start with what the census actually measured. In the United States, every county is divided into smaller census districts. One of them, in Monterey County, is named Big Sur. It begins a few miles south of Carmel and follows the shore past this bridge, far down the coast. Behind the shore, it climbs into the mountains.

Altogether, the district takes in roughly two-thirds of the Big Sur coast. The southern end belongs to a different district, one that reaches over the mountains to a valley inland. Every number we give for the census district is about the outline on this map, and nothing wider. The count itself is from 2020, the most recent census.

The Big Sur district has about 250 square miles of land. Spread its people across all of it. You get about six people per square mile. Wyoming has about the same. No state in the US outside Alaska has fewer people for its size. California, the most populous state in the country, is more than 40 times as crowded.

The county's plan uses a longer ruler. It covers the whole coast, more than 70 miles, from Carmel down to the next county. Keep both outlines in mind, because they don't describe the same ground. To see why the census number is so low, start with the ground itself.

So what makes this ground so hard to live on? Behind the coast rise the Santa Lucia Mountains. At Cone Peak, near the southern end of the coast, they reach 5,200 feet. The county's plan says their western slopes drop precipitously to the sea. That leaves little flat ground for a town, or for a port.

The plan lists what holds building back: water, difficult access, unstable soils on steep slopes, and the dangers of fire and flood.

Take access. Highway 1, the plan says, is the basic route in and out. In 1986, it counted just one other road from inland. That one is a lightly used county road that climbs over the mountains and crosses a military reservation.

Then there's water, which sounds like the odd one out. Nearly fifty separate streams run down these mountains, according to the plan. Yet it calls the water resources small and seasonal. That same water has to support the animals, the plants and the people. There's plenty of it running in the wet months, and much less to count on in the dry ones.

The weather, remember, is mild. The trouble is finding ground where a house can stand, and a way to reach it. That's one reason the census district holds so few people per square mile. The other reasons have more to do with who owns the land, and what happened on it.

About half of the land in the county's plan lies inside the Los Padres National Forest and the Ventana Wilderness. That's public land, run by the federal government, not lots for sale. A wilderness area is land set aside to stay wild, without roads or new buildings. People can hike there, but they can't move in. State parks take up more of the coast, with names like Andrew Molera and Julia Pfeiffer Burns. Homes have to fit on what's left, and much of what's left is steep. In 1986, the plan named the main pockets of homes and shops: the Big Sur River valley, Lucia and Gorda. Most other homes sat in small clusters along ridges and canyons.

And the ground itself can move. In 2017, at a place called Mud Creek, near the southern end of the coast, a whole hillside slid down over the highway. That July, Shawn Harrison, a researcher with the US Geological Survey, flew a drone over the slide. The agency was tracking how the slide kept changing. In his video, the road simply disappears under a new slope of earth and rock.

Mud Creek wasn't the last time. Caltrans, California's highway department, has names for some of the slopes that have closed the road since then. Two of them, Paul's Slide and Regent's Slide, will matter later in this story.

Steep ground, slipping ground, public ground, and not much water. Even so, long before the highway, people made a living on this coast.

So how did they do it? They ranched, mostly to feed their own families. They cut redwoods for lumber, and peeled tanbark for the leather trade. They mined limestone and gold. By the 1880s, the county's plan says, nearly a thousand people lived mostly this way. That count is for the whole coast in the plan, not just the census district.

Some of the original homesteaders left their names on the map: the Pfeiffers, Charlie Bixby, Jim Anderson. The bridge at the start of this video carries Bixby's name. Another homesteader, Bill Post, had a ranch where Big Sur's original post office and its second schoolhouse were built.

There was no highway. The plan says the mountains, the deep canyons and the lack of roads made travel slow and difficult. So most of what the coast produced went out by sea. Small trading boats called at landings along the shore. They loaded lumber, bark and limestone, and they dropped off supplies. Around one of them, Notley's Landing, a thriving village grew up.

Toward the southern end, gold turned up near Alder Creek. A boomtown called Manchester sprang up around it. At its peak, the plan says, it had five saloons, a dance hall and a hotel. By 1895, the boom had begun to fade.

Over land, there was a road of sorts. The plan calls it hazardous, and says it had to be closed part of the year. Around 1900, visitors were already taking a stagecoach in from Monterey to camp in the redwoods. Some locals earned extra money guiding hunters and fishermen from the cities. A road you could count on in every season was decades away.

The idea of a road open all year came from a doctor, John Roberts, who founded the town of Seaside, near Monterey. Work on the coast highway began in 1919, according to the Federal Highway Administration. In 1921, California voters approved more state money for it. It would take nearly two decades in all.

Part of the labor came from prisoners. San Quentin, a California state prison, set up three temporary camps along the route. One stood by the Little Sur River, one at Kirk Creek, and later one at Anderson Creek. The inmates were paid 35 cents a day, and their sentences were reduced.

Machinery blasted through the cliffs. Many of the original settlers, the county's plan says, were enraged by the damage. It describes scarred headlands, and canyons and waterfalls fouled with debris.

The highway was finished in June 1937, for about 8 million dollars, the plan says. Then it sums up the change in one line. A way of life had ended.

The new road made the coast easy to reach for people passing through. Along it grew campgrounds, lodges, restaurants and places to pull over for the view. In 1965, the plan notes, the state named this stretch its first official scenic highway. The road itself was becoming the reason to come. By the 1980s, nearly all summer traffic on Highway 1 was recreational, by the plan's estimate. More visitors raised a harder question for the county, about how much of this coast should be built on at all.

Protection had started even before the highway was finished. In 1934, John Pfeiffer sold land to the state as the core of a new state park. The county's plan marks that sale as the start of the coast's long-term protection. Other families gave land for parks too, and the plan credits their generosity. By 1986, about half of the coastal zone was public land, according to the plan.

That 1986 plan is the one we've been quoting all along. Its basic rule is about what you can see. The county made it policy to prohibit all future development, public or private, visible from Highway 1 and from major public viewpoints. The plan calls everything you can see from those places the critical viewshed.

The test, in the plan's own words, is normal, unaided vision, in any direction, for any amount of time, at any season. If a new building would show, the plan says it had to be moved, redesigned, or not built there at all. New roads and grading were not allowed to scar that view either. Transmitter towers and power equipment had to stay out of sight too. Out of sight of the road, new homes remained possible, under conditions.

The plan treated the road itself as a limited resource. In 1986, it counted about 2.9 million visitors a year. Traffic jams on Highway 1 were already a problem, the plan says. It expected the number of visitors to double. So it set aside most of the highway's capacity for recreation. All the new homes together could use no more than 15 percent of it.

The rule didn't empty this coast. The coast was thinly settled long before 1986. What the plan decided was how the coast should look from the road, and who the road was for. In the 2020s, the trouble was keeping that road open at all.

So what happens to a coast like this when its road breaks? In January 2023, Paul's Slide closed Highway 1. In February 2024, Regent's Slide gave way, six miles to the north. Paul's Slide reopened that summer, but Regent's kept the road cut.

For almost three years, you couldn't drive this coast from end to end. Crews drilled thousands of steel bars into the slope at Regent's Slide to hold it in place. Caltrans reopened the road there at noon on January 14, 2026. The repair was long and expensive, and it finished months ahead of its target date. Even then, Caltrans warned drivers to expect occasional full closures while crews cleared debris.

Fire was on the county's list of dangers, too. In August 2026, a wildfire started in the national forest above the coast. It became known as the Timber Fire, and it spread through these mountains. Air tankers from across California flew missions over the ridges. The state fire agency listed hundreds of homes, businesses and other buildings as threatened. Firefighters were hurt fighting it. By mid-October, it was almost fully contained.

For weeks, Caltrans kept parts of Highway 1 inside the census district closed. Farther south, a second fire, the Plaskett Fire, closed another stretch. By November 2026, the road was open from end to end again, with one-way traffic at a few work zones. Through all of it, there were homes on this coast. The question is who was living in them.

In 2020, the census district had a little under 900 homes. They're scattered along the ridges, the canyons and the river valley. On census day, almost four in ten of them stood empty.

Empty, on census day, doesn't have to mean abandoned. The Census Bureau also runs a longer survey. Its results for 2020 to 2024 put nearly all of the district's empty homes in one category: seasonal, recreational or occasional use. In other words, they're homes people keep, but don't live in. Across California, homes like that make up about a third of the empty ones. In the census district, an empty home usually means a part-time one.

It isn't a new pattern. In 1976, the plan says, about one home in six on this coast stood empty because it was a second home. Housing was scarce for the people who worked there, too. The 1986 plan noted that some had camped out, lived in cars, or moved in with friends.

The visitors are the other side of the count. After the road reopened in 2026, Caltrans reported that the visitors came back. They come for the view the 1986 plan set out to protect. Then they drive on. The census doesn't count them, because this isn't where they live.

So how empty this coast is depends on what you count. Count the people who live in the census district, and it's as empty as Wyoming. Count the homes, and there's room for more people than live there. Count the cars on Highway 1, and you find a road the county was already rationing in 1986.

On a map of this coast, the original homesteaders are easy to find. Bixby is the creek under the bridge from the start of this video. Back then, it was one of the coast's early centers of activity. Pfeiffer is the name on two state parks. One of them began with land a Pfeiffer sold to the state, before the highway was finished. Those early families are part of the map, and part of why so much of it became public land.

The highway across that bridge runs all the way from one metro area to the other. Together, they hold more than 17 million people. In between, the road winds past ridges, canyons, forest and parks. On census day, the census district around the bridge counted fewer than 1,500 people who called it home.
